subject: chemistry
title: Organic Chemistry Adventure: Cracking and Forces
welcome_lead: Today you'll crack long hydrocarbons and explain trends with intermolecular forces.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry stretch — thermal and catalytic cracking, why we crack, intermolecular forces and homologous series.
final_note: You learned why cracking matters, how forces explain alkane trends, and what makes a homologous series.

concepts.def: Breaking long hydrocarbons into shorter useful ones
High temperature and high pressure, no catalyst
Hot powdered catalyst, lower temperature needed
Family with same general formula and reactions
Short-chain liquid fuel in high demand

walkthroughs.body_html:
Crude oil gives too much long-chain heavy oil and not enough petrol.

Cracking chops long alkanes into shorter alkanes (for fuels) and alkenes (for polymers like poly(ethene)).

Example: C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4. One long molecule becomes a petrol-sized alkane plus ethene.

Longer chains have more surface contact with neighbours, so intermolecular forces are stronger.

Stronger forces need more energy to overcome, so boiling point and viscosity go up. Long chains also have less surface exposed for oxygen to attack, so they're harder to ignite.

A homologous series shares three things:

1. Same general formula (e.g. alkanes CnH2n+2). 2. A gradual trend in physical properties as n increases. 3. The same chemical reactions because they share the same functional group.

mcqs.q: Why is cracking carried out in industry?
options: To make crude oil thicker
To turn long alkanes into useful short alkanes and alkenes
To remove sulfur from oil
To increase the boiling point of petrol

mcqs.q: Why do long-chain alkanes have higher boiling points?
options: Stronger covalent bonds inside the molecule
Stronger intermolecular forces between molecules
More double bonds
They contain oxygen

mcqs.q: How do alkenes typically react with bromine?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
Bromine substitutes for a hydrogen on the alkene, releasing HBr.
By electrophilic addition — bromine adds across the double bond to form a dibromoalkane.

mcqs.q: When water boils, what is broken?
options: Intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules are broken — the O-H covalent bonds stay intact.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen atoms are broken when water boils.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
Water molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen gas when they boil.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
